title: How Children Acquire Grammar
subject: soc
paras: By the age of four or five, most children speak in long, grammatically complex sentences, even though no one has given them formal lessons in grammar. How they accomplish this has been one of the central questions of linguistics for more than half a century.

One clue comes from the errors children make. An English-speaking child who has correctly said "went" for months may suddenly begin saying "goed." This mistake is revealing, because the child has almost certainly never heard an adult say "goed." Instead, the child seems to have discovered a general rule, that the past tense is formed by adding -ed, and is now applying it to every verb, including irregular ones. Such overregularization suggests that children do not simply imitate what they hear but actively build rules.

In the late 1950s, the linguist Noam Chomsky argued that the speech children hear is too limited and too full of errors to explain how quickly they learn. He proposed that humans are born with a mental system for language, a kind of universal grammar that sets the basic possibilities for all human languages. On this view, children need only experience to set the details of their particular language.

Other researchers have emphasized the power of learning. Studies have shown that infants are remarkably sensitive to statistical patterns. In one well-known experiment, eight-month-old babies listened to a stream of invented syllables for just two minutes. Afterward, they paid more attention to sequences they had not heard than to the "words" hidden in the stream, showing that they had tracked which syllables tended to occur together. Such findings suggest that much of language structure may be learned from input after all.

Most linguists today accept that both biology and experience matter. Children appear to be born with strong learning abilities and perhaps some built-in biases, but they also depend on rich interaction with caregivers. Children who are rarely spoken to tend to develop vocabulary more slowly, a reminder that the conversations of everyday life are a vital part of how language is acquired.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, what is surprising about children's language development?
opts: Children learn grammar mainly from formal lessons.
Children speak complex sentences without being taught grammar formally.
Children cannot speak in sentences until age five.
Children learn grammar only after they learn to read.
qs.why: …even though no one has given them formal lessons in grammar.

qs.q: Why does the author discuss the word "goed" in paragraph 2?
opts: To show that children have poor memories
To provide evidence that children form general rules rather than just imitating
To criticize adults for speaking incorrectly
To show that English has no irregular verbs
qs.why: Such overregularization suggests that children do not simply imitate… but actively build rules.

qs.q: The word "revealing" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
opts: embarrassing
informative
rare
unusual
qs.why: revealing 意为能说明问题的、有启发的。

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, Chomsky believed that
opts: children learn language entirely by imitation
the speech children hear is enough to explain language learning
humans are born with a mental system for language
grammar should be taught in schools
qs.why: He proposed that humans are born with a mental system for language。

qs.q: What can be inferred from the experiment described in paragraph 4?
opts: Babies cannot hear invented syllables.
Babies noticed which syllables often appeared together.
Babies preferred sequences they had already heard.
The experiment took several weeks.
qs.why: …showing that they had tracked which syllables tended to occur together.

qs.q: The word "they" in paragraph 4 ("showing that they had tracked") refers to
opts: researchers
syllables
babies
sequences

qs.q: According to paragraph 5, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
opts: Most linguists think both biology and experience matter.
Interaction with caregivers is important.
Children rarely spoken to may learn vocabulary more slowly.
Biology alone fully explains language acquisition.
qs.why: 第5段明确说 both biology and experience matter。

qs.q: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas of the passage. Introductory sentence: Linguists have long debated how young children master grammar.
opts: Errors such as "goed" show that children actively construct grammatical rules.
Chomsky argued that an inborn universal grammar explains rapid language learning.
Some invented syllables were used in an experiment lasting two minutes.
Research on infants' sensitivity to patterns suggests much structure can be learned, and most experts now combine both views.
Children usually say "went" before age two.
Formal grammar lessons begin at age five.
qs.why: C、E 是细节；F 与原文不符。
